title: Serverless Cold Starts
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Serverless platforms start function instances on demand. A cold start is the extra latency of provisioning and initialising a new instance before handling the first request.
short: On-demand execution pays startup cost on the first call.
long: On-demand execution pays startup cost on the first call. Keeping instances warm, shrinking packages, and pre-initialising runtimes reduce cold-start latency.
proof: With no warm instance available the platform must load code and initialise the runtime, adding startup time to that request.
consequence: Cold starts matter for latency-sensitive serverless applications.

title: Microservices and Service Decomposition
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Microservices architecture splits an application into small independently deployable services with well-defined interfaces and separate data ownership. It increases autonomy but adds network and operational complexity.
short: Independent services trade local simplicity for distributed complexity.
long: Independent services trade local simplicity for distributed complexity. Each service can be scaled and released independently, but failures and latency become distributed concerns.
proof: Independent deployment follows from separate code and data ownership, while interactions become remote calls that need versioning, discovery, and failure handling.
consequence: The architecture suits large organisations more than small applications.

title: Circuit Breaker Pattern
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: A circuit breaker monitors calls to a remote service and stops sending requests when failures pass a threshold, later probing for recovery. It prevents cascading failures and wasted retries.
short: Stop calling a failing dependency until it recovers.
long: Stop calling a failing dependency until it recovers. Fallback responses and timeouts complement the breaker to keep the caller responsive.
proof: Blocking calls while a dependency is failing lets the caller degrade gracefully and gives the dependency time to recover before traffic resumes.
consequence: Circuit breakers improve resilience of microservice architectures.

title: Idempotency in Distributed APIs
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: An idempotent operation has the same effect whether applied once or several times. Idempotency keys let clients retry requests safely after ambiguous failures.
short: Retries must not duplicate the side effects of a request.
long: Retries must not duplicate the side effects of a request. Recording processed keys with their responses gives the same result on replay of a request.
proof: A unique key plus a record of processed requests maps repeated calls to the original result, so a timeout can be retried without double processing.
consequence: Idempotency is essential for reliable APIs over unreliable networks.

title: Container Orchestration with Kubernetes
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Kubernetes schedules containerised workloads on a cluster, maintains a desired number of replicas, and provides service discovery, rolling updates, and self-healing.
short: Controllers continuously drive observed state toward desired state.
long: Controllers continuously drive observed state toward desired state. Declarative configuration lets operators specify intent rather than imperative steps.
proof: Controllers compare desired and observed state and take actions to close the gap, so failed containers are replaced automatically.
consequence: Orchestration makes large container deployments manageable.

title: Elastic Auto-Scaling
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Elastic auto-scaling adjusts allocated resources to observed demand, adding capacity during spikes and removing it afterwards to control cost.
short: Match resource supply to demand dynamically.
long: Match resource supply to demand dynamically. Scaling policies use metrics such as CPU use, request rate, or queue depth and must account for startup delay.
proof: Monitoring drives replica-count changes that move capacity toward the level needed for the observed load target.
consequence: Elasticity is a defining economic advantage of cloud computing.

title: Distributed Tracing and Observability
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Distributed tracing records a request's path across services as spans carrying timing and causal relationships. It helps diagnose latency and failures in microservice systems.
short: Follow one request across every service it touches.
long: Follow one request across every service it touches. Trace context propagation, sampling, and aggregation are needed to keep overhead manageable.
proof: Propagating a trace identifier through service calls lets spans be assembled into a causal tree, revealing where time was spent across boundaries.
consequence: Tracing is a core observability tool for production distributed systems.

title: The Mars Pathfinder Priority Inversion Incident
subject: Operating Systems
statement: The 1997 Mars Pathfinder mission suffered repeated system resets caused by priority inversion between a high-priority communications task and a low-priority task holding a mutex.
short: A textbook synchronisation pitfall once threatened a planetary landing.
long: A textbook synchronisation pitfall once threatened a planetary landing. A medium-priority task preempted the mutex holder while the high-priority task waited, so the reset watchdog fired. Enabling priority inheritance eliminated the resets.
proof: Flight software traces showed the high-priority task blocked on a lock held by a preempted low-priority task; once the holder inherited the higher priority it finished quickly and the blocking disappeared.
consequence: The incident made priority inheritance a standard consideration in real-time system design.

title: A Database Index Can Make a Query Slower
subject: Database Systems
statement: Adding an index can slow a query when its predicate matches many rows, because random row fetches through the index can cost more than a sequential scan of the table.
short: More indexing is not always faster indexing.
long: More indexing is not always faster indexing. Optimizers use selectivity estimates to decide between an index plan and a scan; stale statistics can make the wrong choice.
proof: A scan reads pages sequentially, whereas an index plan pays an index descent and often one random access per matching row, so a large match set makes the index plan more expensive.
consequence: Index design must follow workload and selectivity rather than the assumption that indexes always help.

title: The High Cost of a Branch Misprediction
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: On a deeply pipelined processor a single branch misprediction can waste more than a dozen cycles, because every younger speculative instruction must be squashed and fetched again from the correct path.
short: One wrong guess can throw away a pipeline full of work.
long: One wrong guess can throw away a pipeline full of work. Branch predictors therefore aim for very high accuracy, and compilers arrange likely paths to be the fall-through path.
proof: When a branch resolves incorrectly the front end discards the speculative instructions and restarts from the resolved target, paying refill and pipeline latency before useful work resumes.
consequence: Misprediction penalties explain why branch prediction is a first-order performance concern.

title: Cache Misses Can Cost More Than Arithmetic
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A main-memory cache miss can stall a core for hundreds of cycles, far longer than the arithmetic it feeds, so data movement rather than computation dominates many kernels.
short: Moving data can be more expensive than operating on it.
long: Moving data can be more expensive than operating on it. The roofline model captures this by comparing attainable arithmetic throughput with memory bandwidth and operational intensity.
proof: Measured memory latencies exceed single-cycle arithmetic latencies by orders of magnitude, and the roofline bound shows when bandwidth rather than compute limits performance.
consequence: Improving locality often yields larger speedups than reducing instruction counts.

title: Little's Law for Queueing Systems
subject: Operating Systems
statement: In a stable queueing system the long-run average number of items in the system equals the average arrival rate multiplied by the average time an item spends there.
short: Occupancy equals arrival rate times average residence time.
long: Occupancy equals arrival rate times average residence time. The identity requires no assumptions about the arrival distribution or service discipline beyond stability and the existence of the averages.
proof: Over a long interval the total time spent by all items equals the area under the occupancy curve, and dividing both sides by the interval length gives L equals lambda times W.
consequence: Little's law relates latency, throughput, and concurrency in servers, networks, and operating-system queues.
